title: Turn off the main water
intro: Leak or burst pipe: shut the main stopcock straight away and limit the damage.

steps.t: Find the main stopcock: usually by the water meter, under the kitchen sink, in the basement or a bathroom recess.
steps.w: If water reaches sockets or the fuse box, only switch off the mains if you can reach it from a dry spot.

steps.t: Turn it clockwise all the way. If it has a lever, set it across the pipe.
Open the lowest tap in the house: a bit more water comes out, then it should slow and stop.
steps.label: Draining
steps.q: After a minute, has the water stopped running?
steps.fix: The valve isn't sealing or there's another one: close the one at the meter or call your water company now.

steps.t: Put the bucket and towels under the leak and mop up the floor.
Take photos of the leak and the damage: the plumber and your insurer will need them.
Call a plumber. If the water comes from a neighbour or shared pipes, tell the landlord or building manager too.

tips: Find it today, calmly, and tag it with a label: in an emergency you won't waste time.
Open and close it a couple of times a year so it doesn't seize when you need it.

title: Clean a tap aerator
intro: Weak or spluttering flow: limescale has clogged the aerator. Vinegar dissolves it.

steps.t: Put the plug in the drain: aerator parts are tiny and roll away in a second.
Unscrew the aerator at the tip of the spout by hand. If it's stuck, use the pliers wrapped in the cloth.
Take the parts apart (screens, flow insert, washer) and line them up in the order they come out.
Put them in the bowl, cover with vinegar and leave for 40 minutes: the limescale dissolves.
steps.label: Soaking

steps.t: Scrub the screens and holes with the toothbrush and rinse under running water.
Hold the screen up to the light: every hole should be open.
steps.q: Are all the holes in the screen clear?
steps.fix: Soak another 20 minutes or clear them with a toothpick. If it's bent out of shape, buy a matching aerator.

steps.t: Run the tap without the aerator for a few seconds to flush out any grit in the pipe.
Refit the parts in order, screw it on by hand and turn the water on.
steps.q: Is the flow even, with no leak at the thread?
steps.fix: If it leaks at the thread, check the washer is in and flat, then tighten a little more.

tips: Recessed aerators need a small aerator key: it often comes with the tap.
In hard water areas do it every two or three months; shower heads clean up the same way.
Take the old aerator to the shop: threads come in different sizes, like [[22 mm]] or [[24 mm]].

title: Clean a sink trap
intro: Slow drain or bad smell from the sink: take off the trap, clean it and refit it leak-free.

steps.t: Clear out the cupboard under the sink and put the bucket right under the trap.
See what type it is: a bottle trap with a cup that unscrews, or a U-bend with two nuts.
Unscrew the cup or the nuts by hand, anticlockwise: the dirty water drops into the bucket.
steps.w: If it's stuck, use the pliers over a cloth and go gently: plastic cracks easily.

steps.t: Empty the trap into the bucket and scrub inside with the toothbrush until it's clean.
Check the pipe going into the wall and pull out any gunk you can reach with your fingers.
Look at the washers: they should be whole, soft and sitting properly in place.
steps.q: Are the washers whole and soft?
steps.fix: If they're cracked, hard or squashed, take them to a hardware shop and get matching ones.

steps.t: Put it all back and tighten the nuts by hand, plus one last quarter turn.
Run the tap for a minute and wipe a sheet of paper under every joint.
steps.q: Does the paper stay dry under the joints?
steps.fix: If it gets wet, line the pipe up and tighten a bit more. If it still leaks, the washer is crooked or worn out.

tips: Take a photo of the trap before you undo it: putting it back becomes easy.
Clean the kitchen trap every six months: grease and food scraps build up fast.
If the pipe in the wall stays blocked, you need a drain snake: if that fails, call a plumber.

title: Bleed a radiator
intro: Warm at the bottom, cold at the top means trapped air: let it out in minutes.

steps.t: Turn the heating off and wait until the radiator is lukewarm.
steps.label: Cool down
steps.w: Water from a hot radiator scalds: let it cool first.

steps.t: Find the bleed valve: at the top, on the side opposite the main valve.
Hold the cloth and the cup under the bleed valve.
Turn the key a quarter turn anticlockwise: you'll hear air hiss out.
Wait until a steady trickle of water comes out, with no bubbles.
steps.q: Is water coming out with no bubbles?
steps.fix: If it's still only air, keep waiting. If nothing comes out, the valve may be clogged: clear it with a pin.

steps.t: Close it clockwise without overtightening.
Check the boiler pressure: usually [[1-1.5 bar]] with the system cold.
steps.q: Is the pressure in the right range?
steps.fix: If it's low, top it up to the value in the manual with the boiler's filling loop.

tips: Start with the radiator nearest the boiler and work outwards.
Do it at the start of winter: the heating uses less energy.

title: Unblock a sink
intro: Slow or stuck drain: plunger and hot water first, then baking soda and vinegar if needed.

steps.t: Take out the plug or strainer and pull out any hair or gunk you can see with your fingers.
Slowly pour [[1 l]] of very hot, not boiling, water straight into the drain.
steps.w: If you've already used a chemical drain cleaner, don't add anything: it can splash back and burn.

steps.t: Block the overflow hole with the wet cloth and keep it pressed down.
Leave [[2-3 cm]] of water in the sink, seat the plunger over the drain and pump hard 15-20 times.
Pull the plunger off sharply and watch whether the water drains fast.
steps.q: Is the water draining away fast?
steps.fix: Plunge twice more. If it's still slow, move on to baking soda and vinegar.

steps.t: If it's still slow, tip [[100 g]] of baking soda into the drain, then [[250 ml]] of vinegar.
Put the plug in and let the fizzing work for half an hour.
steps.label: Fizzing

steps.t: Flush with [[1 l]] of very hot water and watch how it drains.
steps.q: Does it drain now with no standing water?
steps.fix: The blockage is in the trap: take it off and clean it. If several drains are blocked at once, call a plumber.

tips: On a double sink, block the other drain with a cloth while you plunge.
Once a month, hot water and a spoonful of baking soda stop grease from building up.
Never pour frying oil down the sink: let it cool and bin it in a bottle.

title: Unblock a toilet
intro: Toilet won't flush or water's rising: plunger, hot water and soap, an auger only if needed.

steps.t: Don't flush again. Lay old towels around the base of the toilet.
steps.w: Every extra flush can make the bowl overflow: only flush once the water has gone down.

steps.t: If the bowl is full to the rim, bail some water into the bucket: leave enough to cover the plunger.
Push the plunger into the hole at the bottom of the bowl, sealed tight, and press gently first to push the air out.
Pump hard up and down 15-20 times without breaking the seal, then pull it off sharply.
Wait a few seconds and watch whether the water in the bowl goes down on its own.
steps.q: Has the water dropped to its normal level?
steps.fix: Plunge 2-3 more times. If nothing changes, move on to hot water and soap.

steps.t: Squirt in a good dose of dish soap, then [[3 l]] of hot water, about [[60 °C]], poured from a bit of height.
steps.w: Never use boiling water: it can crack the porcelain. Don't combine this with chemical drain cleaners.

steps.t: Leave it 20 minutes: the soap lets the blockage slide and the water softens it.
steps.label: Soaking

steps.t: Plunge again, then flush just once and keep an eye on the water level.
steps.q: Does the toilet flush normally again?
steps.fix: If not, use the auger in the next step. If something hard fell in, don't push it further: call a plumber.

steps.t: Still blocked? Feed the auger into the bend and turn the handle while pushing gently, then pull it out.

tips: If you flush and it rises, lift the cistern lid and push the float down to stop the refill.
A proper toilet plunger has a rubber flange that fits into the hole: it seals far better.
If several drains gurgle or back up together, the blockage is in the main stack: call a plumber.

title: Fix a running toilet
intro: The toilet keeps running: adjust the float or replace the flush valve seal.

steps.t: Lift off the cistern lid (or the flush plate on a concealed cistern) and set it down on a towel.
steps.w: A ceramic lid is heavy and fragile: hold it with both hands and put it on the floor.

steps.t: Check the level: the water should stop about [[2 cm]] below the top of the overflow pipe.
If it's too high, lower the float with its adjusting screw or the clip on the rod, a little at a time.
Flush and let the cistern refill: the fill valve should shut off on its own.
steps.label: Refilling
steps.q: Does the refill stop on its own below the overflow?
steps.fix: If water keeps coming in, the fill valve is worn: replace its washer or the whole valve.

steps.t: Add a few drops of food dye to the water in the cistern and don't flush.
Wait a quarter of an hour without using the toilet.
steps.label: Dye test

steps.t: Look in the bowl: if it's coloured, water is getting past the flush valve seal.
steps.q: Has the bowl stayed clear of dye?
steps.fix: If not, the flush valve seal is leaking: replace it in the next steps.

steps.t: Close the isolation valve under the cistern, flush to empty it and sponge out the bottom.
Release the flush valve, usually with a quarter turn or a small lever, and lift it out.
Remove the old seal, clean the limescale off the seat and fit the new one, sitting flat.
Refit the valve, reopen the isolation valve and test with two full flushes.
steps.q: After refilling, is the bowl still, with no trickle?
steps.fix: Check the seal is flat and the valve properly clipped in. If it still runs, replace the mechanism or call a plumber.

tips: Take the old seal to the shop: every brand has its own size.
If the bowl stays clear after the test and the level is right, you're done: put the lid back.
On a concealed cistern the same mechanism sits behind the flush plate, often with its own valve.

title: Fix a dripping tap or faucet
intro: Drips even when it's off: replace the washer or cartridge and stop wasting water.
gate: I know where the main water stopcock is

steps.t: Close the isolation valves under the sink, turning them clockwise all the way.
steps.w: Don't undo anything with the water on: it comes out under pressure and floods the room.

steps.t: Open the tap to release the pressure and put the plug in the drain so no small screws get lost.
steps.q: Has the open tap stopped running?
steps.fix: The isolation valve isn't closing: shut off the main water before you go on.

steps.t: Work out the type: several turns to close means a washer tap; a half turn or a lever means a ceramic cartridge.
Prise off the coloured cap, undo the screw under it (Phillips or Allen) and lift off the handle or lever.
Unscrew the headgear or the cartridge nut with the wrench, over a cloth so you don't scratch it.
Look at the part: squashed washer or scored cartridge? Take it to a hardware shop to get an identical one.
steps.q: Do you have an identical part, same size and fitting?
steps.fix: Take the old part to the shop: cartridges differ by just a few millimetres, for example [[35 mm]] or [[40 mm]].

steps.t: Washer tap: swap the washer at the bottom, held by a small screw. Cartridge: fit the new one with its lugs in the slots.
Wipe a thin film of silicone grease on the thread and screw it back firmly, without forcing.
Refit the handle or lever, the screw and the coloured cap.
Slowly reopen the isolation valves, then open and close the tap a couple of times.
steps.q: Does the tap stay dry now when it's closed?
steps.fix: If it still drips, the seat is worn or the cartridge isn't seated: take it apart and check, or call a plumber.

tips: Line up the parts in the order you take them off: reassembly is then easy.
If it drips from the base of the lever rather than the spout, replace the O-rings, not the cartridge.
No isolation valves under the sink? Turn off the main water and open a low tap.
